utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, and you may be seated. Good morning to the technicians, to the interpreters; good morning, representatives of the Registry; good morning, counsel. Let me apologise for this delay. But as soon as I learnt that it was not possible to start at 9.20, I tried to inform you about that. I don't know whether you have received the notification on time. As far as I can see, everybody is here and we are ready to continue. Mr. Nikolic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you. The Defence counsel for the accused Milojica Kos calls its last witness, Mr. Zelimir Skrbic. Indirectly, this means that the last, the fifth witness that we had intended to call is not going to be testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Skrbic. Can you hear me well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will read the solemn declaration that is being given to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Please make yourself as comfortable as possible. Approach the microphone, please. Thank you very much for having come. Now you will be answering questions being asked of you by counsel Jelena Nikolic. Ms. Nikolic, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Will you please give us your full name.

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Zelimir Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Will you please state your full date of birth.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: In Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you have any education?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Where did you complete your elementary and secondary school?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I completed elementary school in Jajce and the secondary in Sarajevo. That was a police academy.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you then continue to get education?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. Several top graduates from the police secondary school went to the police academy in Belgrade, which I then graduated from successfully.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When did you graduate?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you also attend some other seminars?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. After the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, we had assistance of the International Community and we worked with the IPTF. I became a graduate of several courses organised by the Swedish and the US governments.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Were you given some certificates?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. I successfully graduated from these courses and I got certificates which further enabled me to continue with my police work.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you have children?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I have two sweetest little girls.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: After graduating, where did you live and work?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I worked in Sarajevo as an educator in the secondary police school, and after having had further education, I became the deputy commander of the police station in Vogosca. This is where I stayed, that is, in this job, until the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I was waiting for a new assignment in the Ministry of Internal Affairs. I went to and stayed with my parents in Jajce, waiting for this new job to start. This did not happen, however.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Jajce?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I think that it was May 1991, until May.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you then leave Jajce, and where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. I left Jajce because there was threat of war, and I reported to the public security centre, and that was in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: That was in 1992. When I received this telegram to report to the nearest security centre, that is where I was sent.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Where do you live today?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: In Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Where do you work today?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: In the school centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What is your job?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I'm a professor at the police academy.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you cooperate with any international organisations?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, it is with IPTF and ICITAP. Also, the SFOR troops also give us assistance in police training.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, let me take you back to 1992, 1993. When you came to Banja Luka, where did you work in 1992, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: In the Security Services Centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What was your assignment?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I was an examiner for logistics.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you have any other assignments?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: When the courses first started, I was a coordinator of these courses or seminars, whatever you call them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Where were these courses held?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: These courses were held outside of the school centre, because we did not have enough room, but it was all organised by the school centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This was in the city?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When did the courses start, if you know? What year?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: As early as the end of 1992, the courses were already under way.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And did they continue, and until when, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: They continue to date.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You said that you were a coordinator?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Will you explain for the Judges what this involved, to be a coordinator in a police academy, police school.

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: That means that I supervise and guide their work. I first have to ensure that everybody attends, and I would also be present there in one class, or sometimes in several classes, and follow their work, supervise their activities outside of the class as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Will you please tell us: Who attended these courses? Who were the personnel who came there?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: These were all individuals, male or female, who had applied for these courses. This would be mostly through -- sometimes it was internal, but I've heard from my colleagues that this was also advertised publicly.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you know what requirements were needed at that time for somebody to be admitted to such a course?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Of course. I know the general requirements and I know special requirements. The general requirements are completed secondary school of the third or fourth degree, completed military service, no criminal record and no -- they had to be citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and a special requirement was that they are not of the age over 30, and they had to have certain physical and mental capacities.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the programme, the curriculum was like?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is the same curriculum that we've had and it continues, with some little changes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you describe this curriculum for the Judges a little bit?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: More recently, we deal with the Geneva Conventions and the international law more than before, and we put more stress on the human rights and freedoms.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately what subjects -- about these subjects in 1993, to what extent were they offered?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: This was all shorter because now the theory part and the practical part each take six months, whereas it used to be three months each. The subjects that are covered were all kinds of laws, and that included the Geneva Conventions, international law, then the Rules of Service, the things that any police officer has to know in order to be able to discharge his work; traffic control, and everything else that is more specialised knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Will you tell us, in 1993, based on your experience and knowledge, what kind of knowledge would this programme provide in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Sufficient for them to be able to carry out their duties as police officers, sufficient, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The level of knowledge, would you describe it as a high level, medium level, low level?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: They could work in these duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: How long did the course take at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Three months of theory and then three months of practical application.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Will you tell us what this practical part consisted of? Because I think the Judges have heard a little bit about the theory part.

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: The practical part consisted in the students going to the various units. They could go to the traffic control unit, to the general -- to the station where they would be put in patrol duties, and the patrols could be also traffic; and then they could be assigned to administrative units or administrative law.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: After the completion of the course, did the graduates receive any kind of certificates?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, they would be issued certificates on the completed course.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What were they after that?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: They were the junior policemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Were they interns? Does that mean that there was a period of internship?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. The rules asked that you had to have six months, up to a year of this residence or internship.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did the people who attend your courses have any experience in police work?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No, as far as I know, because it was the only institution certified to provide this type of training.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you also socialise with or interact with these students?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Of course, throughout their attendance there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Was this usual?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Please explain.

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Can I? In order to be able to supervise them, to see how they have absorbed knowledge, and also what their behaviour was - in other words, whether they followed the rules, the house rules - if a person would -- if some such behaviour would be identified, we would take steps to correct that, and if it would be repeated, then they would be asked to leave the course. So my role was to observe and see whether some of the individuals had the ability to engage in more complex types of work and then recommend such individuals for further training.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you know a person named Milojica Kos?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In the period 1992/1993, when he was attending the course.

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: When he applied for the course to become a police officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you know what his profession was before 1992/1993?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I did not know initially, but I learned from a conversation with him that he was in the restaurant business. You could see that later, obviously, by checking his personal file.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did he apply for the course as a citizen, a regular citizen, or was it because he was a member of the reserve force?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I was not aware of that either, but in a conversation with me, he told me that he had come from that reserve police background. Of course, that could also have been checked in the personal file.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you know him in 1993 when he was a student at the course?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, in 1993, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you know where he attended the course?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: This is, as I said, this was in the student centre, because, as I said before, we did not have enough room. But this student centre had -- was a good enough facility because they could get accommodation there and they could also have class -- they could use classrooms there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In your role as a coordinator, did you have contact with him?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, I supervised them during the classes and I also mingled with them after the classes in order to identify certain qualities in them, and then later on, even later in restaurants and coffee bars, and places like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In your observation of Milojica Kos, in your conversations with him, did he stand out in his behaviour in any way; in classes, outside of classes?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No, he did not stand out. He was one of the crowd. When I say "the crowd," I don't mean this -- it was a group. The comments that he was making were about regular things. He did not show a tendency to go on with the training, but he did complete the training that he had started.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Will you please be so kind and describe the character of Milojica Kos, so far as you remember.

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Outside of classes, he was a regular person, didn't stand out in any way, had a very developed sense of humour, quite developed sense of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. humour. He was a good soccer player. He was good on the -- he was a good attacker, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you have identified in him any leadership qualities?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is all I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'm also going to ask several questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: I'm Krstan Simic, attorney from Banja Luka. Along with Mr. Lukic, we represent Mr. Kvocka's Defence. I'm going to use the opportunity of your presence here as a Defence witness for Mr. Milojica Kos to ask you some questions. Based on your personal knowledge and experience, and you told us that you also worked as a deputy commander of a police station --

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: -- will you give us a classification of jobs within, let's say, a general purpose police station.

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: First is the safety of human lives and protecting the constitutional system, providing security for facilities in your zone of operation; provide crime expertise; control of traffic on roads; control of transportation of hazardous materials and everything else listed in the rules and regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Within your daily tasks in the police station, do you also have duty service?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is part and parcel of our job.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: While we're discussing work of a police station, could you tell us, very briefly, what is its leadership structure?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: From the top down, first there's a commander of the police station, his deputy. Depending on the size of the police station, there may be several assistants. At least one is necessary. And then the organisational part, which consists of police officers, you have uniformed officers, you have the crime service and the traffic department or division, and then also the administrative unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, I would just like to focus on the uniformed part.

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: We have a commander, deputy, one or more assistants, and then uniformed police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Can there be departments or detached departments within a police station?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Depending on the configuration of terrain, depending on the density of population in an area, of course, you can organise detached departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: That would depend, as I said, completely on the density of population in an area. There can be one or several detached departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Based on your personal knowledge and experience during your time spent in the police force, what would be the personnel structure of a detached department of the police station?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: It would have a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Is that all that it would have?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. It would only have a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, within the framework of a general police station, are there also duties that are called a chief, a head of a shift or chief of shift --

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. It depends.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: -- in the basic police station structure?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. There is the head of shift or the chief of shift or duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Now, what about providing security? What does it involve?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: It could be regular security and it could be extraordinary security duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What is the difference between the regular and extraordinary?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: The regular security involves 24-hour round-the-clock security, and that means the presence of the police officers in the police station. Now, this also involves providing security for certain facilities or persons in the area covered by the police station. Extraordinary circumstances means something that is not regular, which would mean large public gatherings, sports events, and other types of events that would be covered until the end of such event is over, and it would also involve a group of persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Who is in charge of providing security for extraordinary events?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: The superior in charge of the area where the public gathering is to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: If a gathering is supposed to take place in Banja Luka, who would be in charge of providing security?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: The superior officer of the Centre of the Public Security Services or the chief of station where the public gathering is taking place. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: It is the commander of the police station in whose area the gathering is taking place who is in charge of the plan, and it is the chief of the Centre of Public Security Station who is in charge of implementing the overall security plan for the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Let us clarify something. My colleague has drawn my attention to a sentence which is missing, that is, a word that is missing from the record, so I will repeat my question so that we can have your answer once again. Who is responsible, who is in charge of functioning extraordinary Security Service in an area?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: As I said, the plan is carried out by the superior officer of a police station, that is, the commander of a police station in whose area the gathering is taking place; and responsible for the overall implementation of the plan is the chief of the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, on the basis of your experience, what do the duties of the duty officer involve? I'm talking about general police station where you were a commander.

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No, a deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Yes, a deputy commander. What is the work of a duty officer? What is his assignment?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: His assignments are the following: He is in charge of receiving all kinds of reports from citizens, both direct reports or anonymous reports. He coordinates work of police officers and dispatches them to their work assignments, depending on the area which is under the control of the police station and depending on where the event took place. He is assigning them to various shifts in the following way: Once a shift begins, there must be a review of police officers. He is the one who has to check on their conditions, both visually and by various questions. He checks on their uniforms and he asks them if there is anyone who does not feel ready to perform their duties, and he also is in charge of checking on their equipment, including police batons, pistols, and all other equipment that they're using. So he is the one who dispatches the shift to their assignment and he is also in charge of coordinating the work of police officers in various shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: The duty officer, does he have a superior position in respect of others?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No, he doesn't. He only implements decisions of his superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, on the basis of your experience, once again, can you tell us if it is necessary, as part of extraordinary security, to organise duty service?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Again, it depends what kind of extraordinary circumstances we're talking about that would require security.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: If that service should be organised, would the work of the duty officer be identical to the work which is performed by the duty officer within a police station?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those tasks are identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: As regards individuals who are not familiar with the system of the work of the police, can the work of a duty officer create a different picture in respect of the officer who is in charge of providing direct security in a given area?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. It can create a different impression. When you're very young or uninformed, if you come across any person in uniform, be it a uniform of a postman or some other officer, you can be under a completely different impression of what their work is. You may think that they are a person of authority. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Mr. Simic. Any other counsel who wish to cross-examine the witness? No. Ms. Somers for the cross-examination, please. I think that you have approximately 35 minutes for cross-examination. Mr. Skrbic, you are now going to answer questions that will be put to you by the counsel for the Prosecution

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, in which canton does Vogosca find itself, please?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the organisation for cantons. I assume that it is in the Sarajevo canton.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, you were deputy commander of Vogosca, and you are not sure of its organisational structure today. Do I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, you understand me correctly. I live in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You mentioned two organisations with whom you do some -- or with whom you have contact or with which you have contact in the International Community; one, of course, is IPTF and the other one was ICITAP; is that correct? That's the International Criminal Investigative Training Assistance Program; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what you mean when you say "investigative training."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You indicated that you had professional deals as a police officer with two international organisations. You gave initials and one of them was ICITAP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: ICITAP.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, when did you first have an association with ICITAP, please?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Two years ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: With which individual in ICITAP have you been dealing, please? Name and location.

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I had contact with him only during the training. His name is William Anderson; he lives in the United States, but I don't know where he is at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Where did that training take place, please?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: It took place in the school centre, in my office.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Which is where?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: The Banja Luka School Centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you receive any type of certificate from ICITAP as a result of this training?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Of course. I have quite a few of them, and Mrs. Nikolic has them all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What was the date of the receipt of the certificate and the date of the training, please?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I think that the exact answer can be found in the documents so I think you should ask Mrs. Nikolic to give it to you, to show it to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm asking you, please. You completed the course work. Would you give us the date? Month and year would be fine.

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: March.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Year, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The documents are all here. With your permission, Your Honour, and if my learned colleague agrees, we can have a look at the document without all these questions and without forcing the witness to remember the exact dates. They're all here in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Nikolic, but I think that Ms. Susan Somers is doing her job. The witness can always say, "I cannot remember." Ms. Somers is just doing her work as counsel for the Prosecution, and I cannot intervene in that respect. The witness has already said that the documents are in your possession and that the facts, the relevant facts, can be checked out. Ms. Somers, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The description of police structure, which you just gave in response to Mrs. Nikolic's questions, was based on your experience in Vogosca, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No, Ms. Nikolic didn't ask me that question. I think it was Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. You're absolutely right. Mr. Simic's question, the answers - and I'm sorry I confused that, my fault - the answers you gave were based, were they not, on your experience in Vogosca as a deputy commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Vogosca, the experience there was prewar, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You have a relative who was with the Ministry of Internal Affairs from the former Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Who is that person, please?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: There are several of us Skrbics in the police. I don't know who exactly you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: A member of the Ministry, a high official. Who would that be, please?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: What exactly do you mean by "a high official"? I don't quite understand your question. Are you referring to the former Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, prewar Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have an uncle, my father's brother. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: His name, please?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Dragan Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What was his position in the Ministry of the former Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: He was a commander of a traffic police station, station number 2, for awhile. I think that later on he was the Chief of the Traffic Safety Department for Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Where was he situated? Where was he based, please?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: In Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Is this the same uncle whose assistance you invoked after assaulting a teacher named Bilic in Jajce in 1991? Do you remember that incident?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No. Bilic in Jajce?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You were 26 years old, were you not, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: If that's what you're saying, then it must be correct. Yes, I was born in 1966.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you were working in Vogosca, which years were those, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So you were 25-ish years old, approximately 25 years old, and you achieved rank of deputy commander. Did you get that with your uncle's assistance?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No, only thanks to my work. I do not rely on the assistance of relatives. I personally hate all kinds of nepotism.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you have difficulties when you were at the secondary police school in Sarajevo because of your temper?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I was not at the police academy in Sarajevo. I attended the Secondary School for Internal Affairs in Sarajevo. I do not have a bad temper; I'm just a vivacious person, if I can say so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The summary which Mrs. Nikolic and her team provided us indicated that you had a diploma from a military academy in Belgrade. Earlier today, I believe your testimony was that you had a diploma from a police academy in Belgrade, or a secondary school. Can you tell us, please, what diploma do you hold from Belgrade, and what type of academy, police or military?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: After each successful completion of any training or school, you always get a certificate or a diploma. After I completed the Secondary School of the Internal Affairs, I received an appropriate diploma, after which, as a student who graduated cum laude, with the help of a state grant, I was sent to a camp, a military academy in Belgrade, which I also completed successfully, and I also have a diploma to that effect. The former Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina educated this type of personnel strictly for police work in order for them to have leadership and commanding capabilities, so that the whole service would be updated.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know an individual by the name of Milenko Sovilj?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Milenko Sovilj?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And does he have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Miki.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know an individual named Dusko Tisman?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Dusko Tisman? Yes, yes, I know him from Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know him from a time when the three of you and others formed the reconnaissance and diversion unit in Jajce municipality at the beginning of 1992? Is that where you know him from -- them from?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you have misrepresented this unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Help me represent it correctly. Describe it accurately, its mission, its composition.

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: You want me to describe its mission and its composition; is that what you want me to do?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If you can.

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: As regards the mission, we didn't have anything special. We were posted in a mountain hut and we were just staying there for awhile.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your relationship with Stojan Zupljanin was close and trusted, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The 27th of October, 1992, roughly, the 26th perhaps, you were involved in the takeover of Jajce municipality, were you not?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: What kind of takeover of municipality are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The Serb victory, as it were - I use the term cautiously - in Jajce. There was a resistance, was there not, by Muslims and Croats which did not prevail. In October, Jajce fell to the Serbs, did it not?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I didn't feel any resistance whatsoever. There was no resistance at all. I entered Jajce normally.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You were in Jajce, though, in October of 1992, when Jajce fell to the Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. I went there because I wanted to see my family. My mother-in-law and my wife's grandmother and her brother were still there, so I wanted to see if they were still alive, and help them, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would the usher be kind enough to distribute 3/213, please. I must apologise for the quality of the copy and to inform the Court, pursuant to its directive, we will try to get the originals presented on short notice. It's a bit difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What you have in front of you, Mr. Skrbic, is a photocopy of a document that was sent by, it appears, packet radio, under the name of Stojan Zupljanin, the head of the CSB in Banja Luka. This document, dated 26 October 1992, discusses, among other things, substitution of various police personnel in Jajce, in assistance to the 2nd Krajina Corps, which was engaged in the takeover of Jajce. Your name appears on the second page as being appointed by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers, I think that the witness has only one page and you have two pages, so when you say "on the second page," you must bear in mind that the witness has only one page.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The Serbo-Croat edition is one page. The English translation, Your Honour -- and I apologise that there has not been yet a French translation. The English translation has two pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, on your page, of course, roughly an inch above the area where Zupljanin's name appears, it reads: "I appoint Brane Pecanac as CSB Security Services inspector, the commander of the company; and Zelimir Skrbic the deputy commander; and someone name Marjanovic the assistant commander." The purpose of this manoeuvre unit which is described on page 1 in the English was what? Can you tell us what manoeuvres police were going to do for the 2nd Krajina Corps and what your role was to be?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The purpose of this manoeuvre unit, which is described on our first page and your first page as well, in assistance to the -- I'm sorry. Can you tell us what manoeuvres the police were going to do for or with the 2nd Krajina Corps and what your role was going to be?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Protection of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Which civilians?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to ordinary citizens.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Of which nationality, which ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Regardless of their ethnicity. A civilian is always a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You were a sniper, were you not, during that operation?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No. I cannot handle sniper at all well enough, the way it should be handled by a professional sniper shooter. I mean, through my training I became familiar with this type of weapon, but no, the information you have is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Explain, please: Why is a manoeuvre unit necessary, a manoeuvre unit in aid of the 2nd Krajina Corps, necessary to protect civilians? Help us understand that, please.

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: So as to prevent the military to act in a brutal manner towards civilians. You know how things are in war: When people lose a member of their family, they act irrationally. They may attempt to murder someone. So we were there to protect the civilians from that type of behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You were there to expel Bosniak civilians, were you not?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know the Hotel Turist in Jajce? Are you familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: As a young man I went there very often, because it's near the lake.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: As a 25-year-old or 26-year-old man, you sniped at Bosniak refugees who were in that hotel, did you not, in October of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you first spoke with Milojica Kos and you found out that he was a reserve policeman, did he tell you that he had worked at the Omarska detention camp or investigation centre?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you ask?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I didn't even know that there was such a camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You were in Banja Luka at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes, I was in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, think hard. This Chamber has heard a lot of evidence about the role of CSB in the camps. Are you suggesting that as a member of the CSB, you did not know the Omarska camp existed?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No, I really didn't know. It was only later that I heard this, from others.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When did you hear it, and from whom, please?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly who it was that told me, his name and surname, but there were stories going round among people in groups that there were certain camps there, and I know nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Just what did you hear about the camp?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Just the fact that it existed, nothing more, and I wasn't interested anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When did you hear about that? Please give us a date, a month and a year, at least.

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Perhaps at the end of 1993, beginning of 1994. No, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you learn about other camps? Manjaca, for example?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. Also through stories, I knew, I heard, that there was a camp at Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When did you hear the story about Manjaca, which is in Banja Luka, near Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: It's near Banja Luka; it's not in Banja Luka. It's a mountain near Banja Luka, some 20 kilometres away. And I heard -- there was a story going round in town that there was a camp there for interrogations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So you didn't know about it. Mr. Kos didn't tell you about it. When you learned about the existence of Omarska, did it occur to you to find out if anyone you were training may have worked there? After all, you had this Geneva Conventions background.

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew about the Geneva Conventions, but because of my own responsibilities, I really didn't have time to inquire about others. I had my own problems to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you telling us that you would give out a certificate of training to someone whose background you knew absolutely nothing about? What, pray tell, is the value of the certificate, if that's the case? Help us understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness never said that he gave anyone certificates. That is drawing conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Susan Somers. Rephrase your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did Mr. Kos complete his training under you?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: He did, as did many others.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And if you allowed him to successfully complete his training, did you feel a sense of responsibility toward the lives that you say policemen are obligated to protect to know the background of those you were turning loose as policemen?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: It is not I who make it possible for them to become policemen. There's a whole team of teachers, and by checking what they know, they give them passing marks or not. And vetting when all these students apply for a job is done by somebody else; it is not part of my responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, you said you supervised Kos in class, did you not, or were you wrong about that?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I didn't observe Kos in the class. Kos is just a dot in the ocean, and I watch them all, and if anyone stands out, either in a positive or a negative sense, I take steps; I reward them or tell them what they need to do to improve.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Well, then, please explain what supervision means to you in a classroom setting. What does it mean to supervise someone like Kos if you know nothing about him?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about any of the students. This is another team of people who check out the physical and mental abilities of the applicants, and it is up to me to supervise their work during instruction, whether they're interested in acquiring the theoretical knowledge that is being given to them at the courses.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that had you made an inquiry and learned about the things that went on in Omarska camp, you might have reconsidered allowing people --

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Every person is assumed innocent until proven otherwise, and the witness said that the candidates were received according to information available. This was in 1992, 1993. The indictment is dated 1995, as Your Honours are well aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this issue discusses behaviour that was prior to 1993, and we are asking about attitudes of a professional, as we've been told, police person, as to whether or not had certain information been given to him, would he perhaps have taken a different course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ask for the information.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If you had learned -- if you had decided to make an inquiry about what took place at Omarska camp and had learned that certain types of injury and violation to civilians occurred on a regular, systematic basis, would that have changed your opinion about any persons under your supervision being fit for police service who may have been in that camp?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question when I don't know what was being done in the camp, whether it in fact existed, nor did I have any interest in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would the usher be kind enough to distribute Prosecution's exhibit that was tendered -- that was admitted under the 1999 binder, 2/316. I'm told that they have been provided for the Chamber. I don't know whether we have sufficient copies for my learned friends opposite, but I can -- I think I might have just enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In front of you, Mr. Skrbic, is a document which bears the name Simo Drljaca at the bottom. Are you familiar with Simo Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I would see him in passing, but not personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The essence of this document, dated 13 June 1992, is Drljaca's comment about the ultimate departure of a special unit Banja Luka Security Services. The report is addressed -- it's on -- I'm sorry. It is addressed to the chief of CSB in Banja Luka. Now, that is the place where you worked, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, and so what?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And the point Mr. Drljaca is making is that after all the difficulties, or alleged difficulties, which were made by members of the special unit from CSB, the Omarska police took control and rid themselves of these problem people. You were at the CSB during this time period, were you?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: But I told you what my duties were, inspector in the centre, and this letter is addressed to the chief of the Security Services Centre. I'm not the chief and I have no idea about this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If the usher would kindly distribute 3/212 [Realtime transcript read in error "3/202".]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, this is Exhibit 3/212, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, 212, Your Honour. It was just distributed to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need to correct the transcript accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes. It is 3/212. It does say "202," to my friends in the court reporters section.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm showing you, Mr. Skrbic, a blank registration form for the International Police Task Force which was created, as you know, under the Dayton Accords. If you will look, please, at page 6 of 14. Page 6 --

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: -- under "B," as in boy, 7, the question asks of the applicant: "Have you ever been arrested, indicted, or summoned into court as a defendant in a criminal proceeding or convicted, fined, or imprisoned for the violation of any law, excluding minor traffic violations?" It does not ask, does it, whether or not you may have participated in conduct which is a violation of the Geneva Conventions, international humanitarian law, or anything like that; is that correct? It does not specifically ask that question.

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So, in principle, would you agree that a person who may have worked in a camp such as Omarska, Manjaca, Keraterm, Gradiska, any number of centres where there are allegations of violations of international humanitarian law, serious violations, would not have to indicate on this form such activity?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your objection, Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My objection is that this is a hypothetical question leading the witness to give a certain answer. There are three hypothetical questions put in one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The objection is overruled. I'm going to allow Ms. Susan Somers to pose her question. As you know, this witness spoke at length about training, about regulations, so we are in the hypothetical area. Put your question to the witness, Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I shall repeat my question for your benefit, Mr. Skrbic. In principle, would you agree that a person who may have worked in a camp such as Omarska, Manjaca, Keraterm, Gradiska, or any number of centres where there are or were allegations of serious violations of international humanitarian law, would not have to indicate on this IPTF application form for vetting his participation in such a place, would he? Would he?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: If that person is working in the police and receives a questionnaire of this kind and knows that he has been indicted by any court, then he would necessarily have to say yes in answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We weren't speaking about indicted. If someone simply worked there and managed to continue walking free afterward, that person is not obligated to indicate his activities or work at such a camp, is he?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, I think the witness has already answered your question. Please go on to your next question and watch the time, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you indicate to IPTF -- I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm looking at my screen and I can't find the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would have to agree that I don't think he answered my question, but if His Honour Judge Rodrigues wants --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But I want to know the answer. So put the question, "I shall repeat my question ..." where you repeated it, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if we have it on the transcript, but I heard the answer. If you don't have the answer, then put the question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Very briefly, if you would.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I repeat it again, Your Honour? I'm terribly sorry to take the time of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If that person is working -- I'm sorry. We weren't speaking about being indicted. If someone simply worked there and managed to continue walking free afterward, that person is not obligated -- MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Krstan Simic, what is your objection? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my learned friend is basing her questions on presumption, that the very fact that somebody was working in one of the camps is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, Mr. Simic, you are here, you heard my response to the objection, and also I could add that you will have a chance to re-examine. We just decided that Ms. Susan Somers should put the question to the witness to obtain an answer, which, in my opinion, was already given on page 29, line 21. But, in any event, we have allowed Ms. Susan Somers to put the question, so why are you objecting now? Please go on with your question, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That person would not be obligated to indicate his activities or work at such a camp, would he? It only asks about indictment or arrest, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: The question is clear. No mention of any camp is made. I don't really know what you're asking me about. The question is quite clear. "Were you ever arrested, indicted, or summoned to a court of law as a defendant in a criminal proceeding or convicted, fined, or imprisoned for the violation of any law, excluding minor traffic violations?"

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: But if you happened to have worked --

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: So the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. The answer is no, you would not have to indicate any such participation in possible violations because you were not arrested or indicted; correct? Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's what I had in mind all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you for the indulgence. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think perhaps we should have a break. How much time, more or less, do you need, Mrs. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About ten minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you, Mr. Simic, do you have any additional questions? No. Perhaps it's better to have a break; otherwise, we'll be under pressure. The interpreters have certain limits; so do we. So we'll have a break, and after that -- or, rather, I will first ask the usher to accompany the witness out before we break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we are now going to have a half-hour break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Mr. Usher, can you have the witness brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us continue. Mrs. Nikolic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Could I ask the usher for his assistance, please. Would you be kind enough to place the original on the ELMO, and these are copies for Their Honours/for the Bench, for the Prosecution, and for the Registry. Your Honours, before I ask for these documents to be marked for identification, these are the originals of diplomas of Mr. Skrbic on the basis of which he is working today and carrying out his duties and which he needs to take back with him. So could the copies later be filed, because without the original documents he cannot continue working. He has to take the originals with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, quite. You can show the originals to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registrar tell me the number of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document will be marked D8/2.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, you have in front of you this document on the ELMO, dated the 22nd to the 26th of February, 1999, which says, [In English] "United States Department of Justice International Criminal Investigative Training Assistance Program. Zelimir Skrbic is hereby awarded this certificate for successful completion of training in Instructor Development Seminar." [Interpretation] Is that this document?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Were you given this document?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, upon the completion of the seminar.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain to the Judges what kind of a seminar it was.

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: There are several such documents; they should all be together.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. But please tell us, with regard to this first one, what does this diploma mean?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: After this seminar, I was considered fully qualified, on the basis of teachers from the United States, to work at the police academy.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we remove this document from the ELMO now, and can I have the number for the next document, please. Could you please show the original to my learned friends from the Prosecution, and here are the copies for Their Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Usher, could you give us the document, please. No, no, the copies.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just check once again. Has this document been marked D9/2? D9/2?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, you have in front of you a second document, a second diploma, which was also issued by the: [In English] "United States Department of Justice International Criminal Investigative Training Assistance Program. Zelimir Skrbic is hereby awarded this certificate for successful completion of training in Instructor Development Course," dated the 5th to 16th of July, 1999. [Interpretation] Could you please tell us whether you were given this diploma?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was given it personally upon the completion of a seminar. We were asked certain questions by the organisers of the seminar and then issued this diploma, qualifying us for work at the police academy.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Were you given a title?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. The title was Instructor, meaning that I was qualified to teach in this area.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask the usher to remove this document and replace it with the third document, please. Also, we have copies for Their Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to interpose an objection on the grounds of relevance, and I will continue at the time of moving to admit, but I see that these are irrelevant to the nature of the cross-examination that was led. Thank you. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, you opened this door, so it needs to be closed. So you may continue, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. May I just check: The number for this document would be D10/2; am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct. This document has been marked D10/2.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic - I do apologise for mispronouncing your name - you have another certificate in front of you, issued by the United States Department of Justice: [In English] "Training Assistance Program. Zelimir Skrbic is hereby awarded this certificate for successful completion of training in Democratic Policies and Procedures course." [Interpretation] The date is April 10th through the 14th, 2000.

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you receive this diploma?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. Upon the completion of the seminar or course, whatever you like to call it, we were all given handbooks, which are applicable to the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, about democratic policies and procedures.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask the usher to assist me once again, please. Is it correct --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me for interrupting, Ms. Nikolic. How many diplomas do you still have?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the last one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I'm not mistaken, this would be marked D11/2. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct. This is document D11/2.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, we have here another certificate in the English language. [In English] "Zelimir Skrbic has accomplished the course Handling of Conflicts. Content: Public appearance technique, mental readiness, influence of stress," et cetera, et cetera. That's issued -- [Interpretation] It was issued by the Swedish National Police Academy, International Affairs. Mr. Skrbic, did you receive this certificate?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the end of the seminar, organised by instructors, teachers, professors, as they are called in Sweden, and after completing that course, I think there were 12 or 13 of us participants who received such a certificate.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you remember when that was, as the certificate doesn't bear a date?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: It was last year, or rather between 1999 and 2000. And in agreement with the same institution, another seminar will be held. They propose that we should go to Sweden to acquaint ourselves with their system of work.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What kind of work was the seminar on?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: The handling of conflicts by peaceful means, control of stress situations, how to handle people under stress so that no force should be used.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions. Could the usher just collect the originals and return them to their owner, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Ms. Nikolic. Judge Fouad Riad, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, good morning. Can you hear me? Can you see me?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Yes, I can hear you well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I have one main question to ask you. In an answer which you gave to the Defence counsel, Mr. Simic, you said that the duty officer, and I quote you, "has no superior over others" -- "is no superior over others; he only implements orders of his superiors." Now, I take it you are a professor, you know what you are saying, and I want you to give us more -- the benefit of your knowledge. How does he -- how is he supposed, as you said, to implement these orders? I'll explain myself. Suppose first someone obstructs these orders or violates the orders. What is he supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: First a little correction. It is not a duty officer. I think you mentioned duty officers, and in the context, it is not the duty officer; it was just a policeman who is on duty. If I can correct you on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... make it, because I mean officer not in the same -- not in the police word. It's the duty -- the duty man.

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: He is supposed to implement the orders, and somebody obstructs his mission or violates this implementation, what is he supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: At that moment, when a police officer refuses to carry out an order by, let's say, not going to the crime scene or something, he needs to report this to his superior on this incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: He cannot go beyond that; only to report? He cannot punish, he cannot force, he cannot take any initiative?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No, he cannot punish. He just transmits to his own superior whether this order was carried out or not. And in our rules of internal rules, any official can report any other fellow official, his own colleague, if he has observed some infraction or violation of the rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good. Now, if the orders themselves are in violation of the law, is he supposed to implement them?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: A policeman who has received from his superior an order, if he identifies any elements of a criminal act in what he has been told to do - and we are talking about a trained officer - if he, in other words, identifies elements of crime, he is duty-bound to point it out to the superior and then asks to be given such an order in writing, and he should then refuse to carry it out. Of course, he should ask it in writing so that in disciplinary proceedings that were to be instigated, launched afterwards, that he would have a document that he could support his claim with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes, but -- I mean, in the end, he could refuse to do it, whether in writing or oral.

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. May I say that he shall refuse if there are any elements of criminal acts in this order. Of course, I am talking about a trained policeman who is familiar with the law and who knows about the criminal act as set out in the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, apart from refusing to do it, can he take any measure to report it to higher authorities?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Of course. By the very fact that he asks that the order be repeated in writing, he is pointing out that he has identified some elements of an offence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Because you said he needs it in writing just to defend himself if he is being disciplined. But can he take the initiative to raise it with the higher authorities, to say, "My direct superior ordered me to do that," and then the chain of action becomes? What do you think or what do you know?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Of course he can do that. He can also do that orally. But in order to follow the procedure, in order for a police officer to protect himself, it is preferable for him to ask for this order to be issued in writing too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I gather that you are telling me about your system, not what is in this certificate.

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am talking about the system that I am familiar with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Riad. Madam Judge Wald has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, in one of your answers, when you were talking to Mr. Simic about police practices - I assume your answer is based upon your experience when you were a deputy commander - you used both the phrase "duty officer" and the phrase "chief" or "commander of the shift." Now, my question to you is: Based on your police department or police station experience, is a duty officer different from a shift commander; and if so, how?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: A duty officer in a station, as I pointed out before, is the one who handles all the citizens' reports and everything else. We have that in the record. But the shift commander or the chief of a shift is a person who directs police officers to certain duties, gives them certain tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Fine. If I understand you - and if not, correct me - a shift commander, in your view, as opposed to, as different from a duty officer, may give orders directly to the people underneath him in carrying out the shift's functions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No. He only directs them. Each police officer knows what his duties are, so he could be perceived as a sort of coordinator. He just oversees them, supervises whether the orders which had been issued by the superiors are being carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But, as an experienced officer, Mr. Skrbic, I'm sure you're aware that many times situations arise out in the field or they arise out on the street that cannot be anticipated in every detail by the commander ahead of time, so certain action has to be taken. Are you saying that if a new situation that nobody could have anticipated arises and the shift commander is there or is accessible to the men on his shift, that he can't order them or direct them what to do?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: He cannot order them. He can only report to his superior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, excuse me, I mean, I too have a little experience with police work. If you are out in a fire or a violence, a situation on the street, and you have several policemen and you also have the shift commander there, are you suggesting if the shift commander says, "Policeman A, you go over and do this; policeman B, you come around the back and do this; policeman C, you go get this," in order to take command of the situation, that he can't give any of those orders? He has to call back and see if he can reach the commander in an emergency situation? I mean, there has to be some discipline or command in situations that could not have been anticipated ahead of time. Or at least any police work I've ever been acquainted with, and I'm sure it's in these courses too, there has to be somebody who takes over a situation that was not anticipated. Is that completely different in your system?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: You see, you are pointing out -- you're talking about a shift commander being in the field with the patrol, whereas the shift commander is not usually out in the field. There is a patrol leader who is out in the field, and he is the one who gives instructions to his partners in the patrol how best to intervene so that the best results can be achieved, both for the police officers and the person who may be involved in an act of violence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So the patrol leader can give -- whether you call them directions or orders, the patrol leader who is out in the field with the men can give some orders in an emergency situation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. In theory, yes, he can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. My last part of the question is: Now, suppose a few patrolmen, not a patrol leader, but suppose a few policemen are out in the field and a situation arises and they don't know what to do, it is not covered by a specific order, and they call back to the police station, okay? Now, who at the police station, apart from the commander, is authorised to give them advice or tell them what to do in the situation? Let's assume the commander is unreachable for the moment. Who back at the station can tell them what to do in a situation when they call back for advice or direction?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: The policemen should be sufficiently trained to assess the situation and act without any consultations. If they are calling back, that means that they are asking for reinforcements, that they do not have enough manpower or something to handle the situation that they are in, so they are calling in only for reinforcements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, that may be true in your system, but in our system, even the FBI calls back in to headquarters to get advice or direction in an unanticipated situation. You're saying that none of these people out in the field can ever call back to the station and say, "Well, here is option A or option B. Which do you think I should do?" They never do that?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I did not say that they never did, I only said that they should be sufficiently trained to deal with the situations that they encounter. Of course, in extraordinary situations, it may be different. Now, this is all pure theory that I'm discussing here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
