utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Skrbic, I, too, have a few questions for you. You would perhaps agree with me that a carpenter uses his tools in order to carry out a certain task within the framework of his job, his profession; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: You mean -- can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was actually talking about a carpenter. In order for him to be able to do his job, he has appropriate tools for that; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Of course I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are a professional police officer. What is the tool of a police officer, in your opinion? What is a typical tool that a professional police officer uses? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: All tools provided for in the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that you are very able as a speaker. I thought that you would probably answer that his tool is either a weapon or a truncheon. But can it be considered that he has also his person as a tool of his work which enables him to accomplish his job and his profession?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I did not get any translation. I only heard your voice and that was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you agree with me that the professional tool of work of a policeman is his very person?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, it involves his physical fitness, and then there are also his tools of coercion. But then I would also include, I don't know, his whistle, his belt, down to his underwear, if you will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The ability to persuade someone, the ability to communicate with others, does that play a certain role in his work?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Of course it does. Our law strictly provides that one of the means of coercion is verbal skills. For instance, a policeman can verbally try to stop somebody from proceeding with certain acts where that may result in some criminal act.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, I think we've come, finally, to my question. What is the place, within the framework of training and supervision of police trainees, what is the place which is afforded to the personality development, that is, to the qualities which are necessary to communicate with others? That is to say, is it necessary for you to know that person, to have known that person for awhile, even before, in order to know whether that person will make a good police officer?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: As I said, another team was involved in that. My duty was to monitor their performance in the course itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I think that we already discussed the issue, to a certain extent, when we talked about the diplomas. Was there a meeting which would be organised for you to discuss whether such and such person would be a good police officer? Did all of you provide your opinion on the candidate individually? How was it organised?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No. This would be done in the teachers council. Each one of them would cover a certain subject and then would provide their opinion of a student. This would be the participants of the academy or one of the courses. And that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us try and be more direct. As regards Mr. Kos, the person who was in charge of knowing his personality from before, did you share his opinion with -- did you share his opinion?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In response to a question which was put to you by Ms. Somers, you said that you had come to Jajce at one point in time as a police officer [In English] to prevent soldiers to act in a brutal manner towards civilians. [Interpretation] What do you think? What is your opinion? Can police prevent soldiers from behaving in that manner?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: To be honest with you, this depends on the situation. The role of the military is to be at the front line, and in an urban environment it is the police force that has the primary role of protecting lives of civilians. That means that only smaller groups of soldiers would be in an urban environment and the majority would be at the front line. In this environment, the police force would be able to carry out the task of protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You told us that you had heard about the Omarska camp sometime in 1993. Did I hear you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, in 1993, during 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where were you at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: At the school centre. I was a teacher in the rules --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards the training of the police, as regards the educational system of the police, did you have to familiarise yourself with the situation elsewhere? Did you have to know what was going on in another centre?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: That was not in my job description. For me, it was to continually educate myself and to transmit this knowledge to the participants of courses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're telling me that at the time you were teaching, you were actually limited; you were focused only on your personal experience as a police officer?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was involved strictly in my own work, and then outside of that it was my family, to be with my family as much as I could. I continuously educated myself, though, by reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not what I'm talking about. I think I understood you as saying that you were teaching only on the basis of your professional experience. Did I understand you correctly or not?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: On the basis of my experience, what I learned during my own training and later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. So would it have been interesting to acquire knowledge as to the functioning of camps, since the police force was responsible for providing security to such camps; it was one of the police tasks? I think, of course, that it's a rather exceptional situation, but I would like to know whether knowledge about such camps would be helpful for the purposes of training of future police officers.

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Well, this is what is also mentioned in the Geneva Conventions, that nobody has the right to set up camps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're not answering my questions. Maybe I'm not making myself clear. Let us take an example. You have to teach on the basis of your personal experience. You also mentioned that your approach was a scientific one. We have seen a number of your diplomas. I would like to know whether the knowledge of the history of camps and the knowledge about the function of the police within such systems would be interesting, would be helpful for the formation and training of future police officers. Do you now understand my question?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I understand you completely. In the training courses, there is no mention anywhere about setting up of any camps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. I am not going to pursue with this question. You are a professional officer by training. How do you establish a link between the task that you have to accomplish and what do you think that a policeman has to know in order to be able to carry out his tasks? And you have told my colleague, Judge Wald, that police officers have to be successfully trained to react in certain conditions, and, on the other hand, you have your own professional and personal experience. If you were a lecturer, if you teach only on the basis of your personal knowledge, it would be an ideal situation, but if you teach only on the basis of your personal knowledge and personal experience, then you're running a risk of not providing them with sufficient insight in the profession. So I would like to know whether the knowledge, your knowledge of what happened in concentration camps, in particular in Omarska, would that knowledge of yours be useful for your training purposes?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Of course it would have been interesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but that is not a kind of conclusion that you're obliged, that you have to draw; this is something that you know one way or another.

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: What did you mean by that, that I was not duty-bound? I feel that you have sort of put the answer in my mouth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to make sure, if you had answered yes, I wanted to know whether it was because I had led you to provide me that answer or because you indeed understood what I meant by my question.

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I did, I really did understand your question, and I very clearly answered it. There can be no mention of any camp in the courses because it is not in the rules; it is against the Geneva Conventions. Now, and your question to me was whether it would be interesting to discuss the existence of camps with the participants of a course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't wish to open a debate about this issue. I just wanted to know whether -- by knowing what happened in a camp, and in view of the type of security tasks that the police officers were involved in that respect, I think that we can learn, that future police officers can learn something very valuable from that experience, that such conduct is not permissible or acceptable, and similar. Do you see the meaning of my question?

utterances.speaker: ZELIMIR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I think that I have already agreed with all of that, that that was -- that did not exist in the police establishment and maintenance of camps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Thank you very much, Mr. Skrbic, for having answered all of our questions. You have come to the end of your testimony here. Let me ask the usher to accompany you out of the courtroom. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, and if I'm needed, we'll see each other again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Nikolic. You have documents to tender?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I would like to ask that these documents be tendered in the record, that is, exhibits that have been marked D8/2 through D11/2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. Any objections? Ms. Somers, you too have documents to tender, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We would -- well, shall I address our documents or the objections to theirs first? If I may, on the Defence's documents, the questioning on ICITAP was not because we wanted to see any type of diplomas; it went to issues of credibility. The diplomas date to a time well after the issues of Mr. Kos's involvement at Omarska camp and as such are irrelevant to any training that may have been given to Mr. Kos. They are post-Dayton training in a whole different type of policing, democratic policing, which may or may not have taken root. The relevance, I think, has not been established. On D11/2, there is no date. That is the Swedish document. I wanted to bring that to the Chamber's attention. So we have no idea when that particular certificate came through. But again, our objection is grounded in relevance as to what was supposedly imparted to Mr. Kos as a trainer to a trainee. On our two - I'm sorry - the documents which the Prosecution wanted to move into evidence, the 3/212 was the IPTF application, which I think is relevant to whether or not an individual can have continued in policing, even in the absence of a conviction, because the prior testimony has suggested that IPTF certification is indicative of, as it were, a clean bill of health.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers, the documents, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: 3/212 and 3/213. Those are the two documents. The third one was in the previously admitted group. I think it was 2/316 that was the one that was previously admitted, and we simply had it recalled for the Chamber's observation. So today only two are sought as new documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nikolic, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one point, Your Honours. The diploma certificates that have been shown to the Trial Chamber and to the witness, as you yourself pointed out, it was the Prosecution who opened the door by questioning the education.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Ms. Nikolic, I just wanted to know whether you had any objections as regards the documents of the Prosecutor. We have already dealt with this other issue. So 3/212 and 3/213.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honours. I think I misunderstood you. As far as those exhibits are concerned, no, we have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber will admit the documents into the evidence, that is, Defence Exhibits D8/2 through D11/2 and Prosecution Exhibit 3/212 and 3/213. I think that's it for the moment. Let me consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will have our Status Conference, and I think that we should be able to finish by 3.00, which means that I will be more strict than usual in my treatment of questions and issues. I have been working since 9.00 and the Chamber has other commitments today. We will come back at 2.00. So we will have our regular lunch break and come back at 2.00 for the Status Conference.
